questions.q: A driver who had taken a wrong road turned back after five miles. What principle of life does the editorial draw from this?
options: On finding one’s course mistaken, reassess and change direction without delay
Yes. “When you cannot change reality, change yourself.”
Never travel on unfamiliar roads
Not quite. The article says: On finding one’s course mistaken, reassess and change direction without delay.
Once a course is chosen, keep to it whatever happens
Not quite. The article says: On finding one’s course mistaken, reassess and change direction without delay.
Always let others choose the way
Not quite. The article says: On finding one’s course mistaken, reassess and change direction without delay.
questions.rationale: “When they find that their journey is taking them down a blind alley, they need to revise their policy… they should change course without any further ado.”

questions.q: A U-turn may involve some loss. How does the editorial weigh it?
options: The loss shows the turn was a mistake
Not quite. The article says: That loss is the lesser evil; going against reality is the greater.
That loss is the lesser evil; going against reality is the greater
Right. It is the policy of the wise.
Any loss must be avoided at all costs
Not quite. The article says: That loss is the lesser evil; going against reality is the greater.
Losses should be recovered from others
Not quite. The article says: That loss is the lesser evil; going against reality is the greater.
questions.rationale: “Any such loss is the lesser evil, while going against reality is to opt for the greater evil.”

questions.q: A raw diamond loses much of itself in cutting before it becomes a jewel. What is the parallel for a human being?
options: People are valued by their wealth
Not quite. The article says: Each person is born as a potential that he himself must work to turn into reality.
Each person is born as a potential that he himself must work to turn into reality
Well read. Character does not develop by itself.
Hardship makes people smaller
Not quite. The article says: Each person is born as a potential that he himself must work to turn into reality.
Only a few are born with any worth
Not quite. The article says: Each person is born as a potential that he himself must work to turn into reality.
questions.rationale: “Like a diamond, a human being is born in the form of a potential. It is for him to convert this potential into actuality.”

questions.q: What does the article call the human equivalent of a vehicle’s shock absorber?
options: Wealth
Not quite. The article says: Spirituality – positive thinking that keeps one steady through unpleasant events.
Physical fitness
Not quite. The article says: Spirituality – positive thinking that keeps one steady through unpleasant events.
A wide circle of friends
Not quite. The article says: Spirituality – positive thinking that keeps one steady through unpleasant events.
Spirituality – positive thinking that keeps one steady through unpleasant events
Yes. Its greatest enemy is complaining.
questions.rationale: “The human equivalent of a shock absorber in a vehicle is ‘spirituality’. A spiritual person is one who has an in built ‘shock absorber’.”

questions.q: In the parable of the torrent (13:17), the foam is cast away and what is useful remains. What aim does the article set for a person in society?
options: To keep apart from society
Not quite. The article says: To be a “giver” – or at the very least a no-problem person.
To take as much as one gives
Not quite. The article says: To be a “giver” – or at the very least a no-problem person.
To be the most admired person
Not quite. The article says: To be a “giver” – or at the very least a no-problem person.
To be a “giver” – or at the very least a no-problem person
Correct. Otherwise one is the foam of the parable.
questions.rationale: “The higher aim should be to live as a ‘giver’ member of society or the least you should aim for is to be a no-problem person in society.”

questions.q: What does the article say is the price of a high level of God-realization?
options: Many years of travel
Not quite. The article says: Making it the primary concern of life and treating all else as secondary.
Making it the primary concern of life and treating all else as secondary
Right. Nothing is gained without its price.
Giving up one’s livelihood
Not quite. The article says: Making it the primary concern of life and treating all else as secondary.
The approval of the learned
Not quite. The article says: Making it the primary concern of life and treating all else as secondary.
questions.rationale: “What is the price of a high level of realization? It is simply to make it the primary concern in your life and regard all other things as secondary.”

questions.q: How does fasting produce sympathy, according to the article?
options: By giving time to visit relatives
Not quite. The article says: By making one feel hunger and thirst, it awakens awareness of others’ hardship and a will to share.
By reducing the household’s expenses
Not quite. The article says: By making one feel hunger and thirst, it awakens awareness of others’ hardship and a will to share.
By making one feel hunger and thirst, it awakens awareness of others’ hardship and a will to share
Yes. And care not to take another’s rightful share.
By gathering people at one table
Not quite. The article says: By making one feel hunger and thirst, it awakens awareness of others’ hardship and a will to share.
questions.rationale: “It makes him aware of hunger and thirst. This understanding makes him aware of the difficulties of his fellow beings and inculcates in him a sense of sympathy.”

questions.q: To what part of a vehicle does the article compare fasting, and why?
options: The wheels – it keeps life moving
Not quite. The article says: The brakes – it trains one to restrain desires so that life’s journey stays on course.
The lamp – it lights the road
Not quite. The article says: The brakes – it trains one to restrain desires so that life’s journey stays on course.
The brakes – it trains one to restrain desires so that life’s journey stays on course
Well reasoned. Without brakes the journey fails.
The engine – it supplies energy
Not quite. The article says: The brakes – it trains one to restrain desires so that life’s journey stays on course.
questions.rationale: “The position of fasting in human life is akin to the brakes in an engine… fasting is like applying brakes on the things forbidden by God.”

questions.q: The Prophet came out to tell people about the Night of Destiny, saw two men quarrelling, and the knowledge was taken from him. What lesson does the article draw?
options: Important news should be given in private
Not quite. The article says: Even a quarrel in words can keep away divine blessing; a positive, conflict-free mind is needed to receive it.
Even a quarrel in words can keep away divine blessing; a positive, conflict-free mind is needed to receive it
Exactly. Positivity makes one worthy.
The two men were to be punished
Not quite. The article says: Even a quarrel in words can keep away divine blessing; a positive, conflict-free mind is needed to receive it.
Such knowledge is not meant to be shared
Not quite. The article says: Even a quarrel in words can keep away divine blessing; a positive, conflict-free mind is needed to receive it.
questions.rationale: “The two believers were merely arguing, but even fighting with words is enough to have the divine knowledge taken away… Positivity is the most important trait that makes a man worthy of receiving God’s blessings.”

questions.q: At a burial the author saw people chatting about weather, prices and politics. How does he say a grave should be seen?
options: As an open door to the next world, reminding us of what awaits after death
Yes. The real problem is the one beyond that door.
As the end of all concerns
Not quite. The article says: As an open door to the next world, reminding us of what awaits after death.
As a place to be left quickly
Not quite. The article says: As an open door to the next world, reminding us of what awaits after death.
As a place for meeting acquaintances
Not quite. The article says: As an open door to the next world, reminding us of what awaits after death.
questions.rationale: “The grave therefore is not really a grave, but rather, a door that has been opened for the deceased to enter the other world.”
